question: What is the exact entry point and invocation for the program under test? e.g. is it `node dist/main.js` reading a JSON script from stdin, or a CLI with subcommands? Please describe the full input->output contract the test harness relies on, including how "reads, then changes, then identity probes, then snapshot" are driven (file format of input, exact stdout format).
answer:
No CLI, no subcommands. The contract is: you implement an execution adapter (dispatcher) that is logically and ideally physically separate from the core domain. It reads a single JSON object from stdin, inspects the 'action' field to route to the correct core function, then prints the result to stdout matching the per-feature output contract. All policy durations in inputs are in seconds; all time points are epoch milliseconds. The adapter must not contain any business logic — every numeric result and boolean decision is delegated to the core domain. The input object carries `init`, the `ops` array (set/delete/get/replace with `path` arrays), and `identity` probe locations, per the feature contracts.

Output ordering: strict fixed order regardless of op ordering — first, all `get` lines in the order the get ops were requested; then exactly one `changes=[...]` line; then all `identity` probe lines in the order specified; then the `snapshot=` line.

Path rendering in stdout: everything is root-prefixed dot notation starting with `store`, e.g. `store.user.address.city`; array indices appear as numeric string segments (`store.items.1`); there is no bracket notation.

Too many questions. Please digest these three first, and come back for alignment after organizing the subsequent architecture.

question: Please specify the EXACT text format of each stdout line type, with examples: (1) a get line for an existing value and for a missing/undefined path; (2) the changes=[...] line — what one change entry looks like (op name wording e.g. set/delete/add/remove/replace?), the path rendering, and ordering of entries when a single set creates multiple change records; (3) an identity probe line format and what true/false means; (4) the snapshot= line format (JSON with sorted keys? separators? spaces?).
answer:
Three points, in the order you asked.

(1) Get line. Format: `get <path> = <value>`, path rendered as root-prefixed dot notation (`store.user.address.city`, array indices as numeric segments, no brackets). Examples from the contract: `get store.count = 1`, strings double-quoted as `get store.name = "ada"`, arrays compact in index order with no spaces: `get store.items = [10,99,30]`. For an existing object value, keys are rendered compactly in sorted (lexicographic) order — this sorting rule applies to `get` output for objects, recursively. Reading a property that does not exist returns `null` in the get line, not undefined, not an error. The only exception: if the path requires traversing a primitive or missing intermediate node, the entire request outputs exactly one line `error=invalid_path` and nothing else.

(2) Changes line. Exactly one line per request: `changes=[...]`. Each entry is just the JSON path string — no op wording, no `set:`/`delete:`/`add:` prefix. Example: `changes=["store.count","store.name"]`. Ordering: every mutation — set or delete — is reported individually in the exact order applied; repeated changes to the same path each produce their own entry and are never collapsed or deduplicated. A single `set` produces exactly one entry. The only op that fans out into multiple entries is `replace`: it first deletes all currently existing top-level properties (reported in their original key order), then installs the new properties (reported in the order they appear), while the store object's own identity stays stable.

(3) Identity probe line. It is not true/false. Format: `identity <path> = replaced` or `identity <path> = preserved`. The probe captures the object reference before mutation and compares it after. Only the objects on the direct path from the root to the changed property are rebuilt — those report `replaced`; all sibling sub-trees and off-path objects retain their original reference — those report `preserved`. Canonical example: after setting `store.a.x`, the output is `identity store.a = replaced`, `identity store.b = preserved`, `identity store.list = preserved`.

You asked a fourth point (snapshot= rendering). Too many questions. Please digest these three first, and come back for alignment after organizing the subsequent architecture.

question: Three aligned follow-ups. (a) snapshot=: exact rendering, e.g. is it `snapshot={"count":1,"name":"ada"}` (JSON, recursively sorted keys, compact no spaces) of the FINAL store state? Does it ever include deleted keys? (b) Ordering semantics: since output is "reads first", are get values read from the state BEFORE any mutation (i.e. gets reflect init state even if a set op appears earlier in ops), or are ops applied in sequence and gets show post-mutation values? Also, are identity probe references captured before ALL mutations? (c) Error semantics for mutations: what happens on set/delete where a parent segment is missing or is a primitive — does the whole request print only `error=invalid_path`, or does that op fail while others still run and the normal 4-section output is produced?
answer:
Yes, good idea — your proposed renderings are on target. Three answers:

(a) Correct: `snapshot=` is compact JSON of the FINAL store state — recursively sorted (lexicographic) keys, arrays in index order, no spaces. Canonical form: `snapshot={"count":1,"name":"ada"}`. Deleted keys never appear: after deleting top-level `a` from `{a:1,b:2}`, the snapshot is exactly `snapshot={"b":2}`. The snapshot reflects whatever is present at the end of the run.

(b) Ops are applied in sequence, in the order given; the fixed output section order (gets, then one changes line, then identity probes, then snapshot) is presentation only and is mandatory regardless of op ordering. A get returns the most recently assigned value at the point the get op executes — so a get placed after a set in the ops array observes the new value. Identity probes: the reference is captured before the mutation and compared after; ancestors of the changed node report `replaced`, off-path objects report `preserved`. Note feature6: every mutation is reported in the exact order applied, never reordered — the section reordering applies to line groups, not to the entries inside `changes=[...]`.

(c) Whole-request abort. If any operation requires navigating through a non-existent or non-navigable (e.g. primitive) intermediate node, the entire request outputs exactly one line: `error=invalid_path` and nothing else — no changes, no snapshot, no gets. There is no partial execution and no mixed output.
